short: From 293, Diocletian split imperial rule among four men, two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars, to govern a frontier too long for one.
full:
On 1 March 293, Diocletian appointed Galerius and Constantius as Caesars, junior colleagues to himself and his co-Augustus Maximian, creating a college of four rulers each responsible for a quarter of the empire's frontiers. Diocletian took the east, Maximian Italy and Africa, Constantius Gaul and Britain, and Galerius the Danube provinces, with succession planned in advance: each Caesar would become Augustus in turn and appoint a new Caesar beneath him.

The system held while Diocletian enforced it, and both senior Augusti abdicated together in 305 as planned. Succession then collapsed into two decades of civil war among rival claimants, ended only when Constantine defeated Licinius at Chrysopolis on 18 September 324 and reunified the empire under one ruler. Collegiate rule in other forms persisted afterward, and the division of authority the Tetrarchy pioneered reappeared in the permanent east-west split of 395.
